note:
Your ask (9 Oct): detailed timing logs in every job; the unit job more granular too, if that costs little performance; and no job uniquely more detailed than the others, all at about the same granularity.

What's there today:
- Only the unit job times its phases ("piece copied from the NAS: 9s", "DEM cache slice: 34s", …), and ~10 % of its time is still untimed.
- terrain, pack, heritage, pass-sets, water, trees, peaks and the rest log a total and a few counts at most.
- First look, from the build Mac's last 80 h: terrain 7.3 h, unit 6.3 h, pack 2.7 h, heritage 2.7 h, trees 2.3 h, water 1.8 h, pass-sets 1.6 h, peaks 1.5 h. Inside the unit job (52 runs), about 40 % is moving files to and from the NAS (base pack written 18 %, DEM cache slice 16 %, layers staged 8 %, DEM samples kept 6 %).

Feeds #131 (profiling and speeding up the job code).
reply:
Done and published 9 Oct 11:07 UTC (20261009-1107-2b5b5aa): every job kind the agent runs is timed by one rule, terrain and slope included.
- One phase timer for Rust, Python and the pages' tasks: each phase's wall time and CPU, its class (NAS read, NAS write, disk, network, compute, wait), bytes and files; a child program's phases nested under it.
- The rule: every bulk move and every compute stage its own phase, loops summed, no phase per tile; under 5 % untimed. Measured: 0–4.1 % untimed on every sampled kind; the timer costs under 0.01 % (0.2 % on runs under 0.2 s).
- Every job's log ends with the same table; each run's record goes to the lead (coord/timings.jsonl), helpers' and pages' too.
- `scenic timings [kind] [--last N]` shows each kind's phases, totals and shares on either Mac.
- First findings, now #131's: units spend much of their time staging layers and reading their neighbours' kept elevation samples whole; pack jobs copy base packs back; the catalog stats 8,300 files one by one; peaks reload z12 tiles.
text: Detailed timing logs in every build job, at about equal granularity across all jobs
